claims.text: Controlled thermomechanical treatment using systematic rolling and annealing can improve phase stability, refine microstructure, and optimize material properties.
The initial cast or as-processed alloy may have a suboptimal phase distribution and a relatively coarse microstructure.
A thermomechanical processing route can combine rolling deformation and annealing thermal exposure.
Processing across temperatures from non-equilibrium to near-equilibrium, with controlled strain rates, permits simultaneous assessment of phase changes, grain refinement, and property variations.
The interplay of thermal energy and mechanical deformation induces grain refinement and phase transformation.
Controlled thermal activation combined with deformation increases dislocation density.
Controlled thermal activation combined with deformation promotes phase transformation.
Increased dislocation density and promoted phase transformation lead to refined grain structures and stabilized desirable phases.
The resulting refined and phase-stabilized microstructure improves mechanical and potentially functional properties.
Combined rolling and annealing will produce greater phase stability and a finer, more uniform microstructure than isolated heat treatment or deformation.
Combined rolling and annealing will enhance strength and ductility relative to isolated heat treatment or deformation.
Conventional processing using heat treatment or deformation independently produces less tailored microstructures and property profiles.
Improvements may be limited if processing conditions do not adequately span non-equilibrium to near-equilibrium regimes.
Different alloy chemistries may respond differently to the applied thermomechanical parameters.
The proposed thermomechanical mechanism is generally well supported in materials science.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the alloy system and requires empirical tuning of processing parameters.
X-ray diffraction can be used to identify phases and assess phase stability.
SEM or TEM can be used to characterize microstructure and grain size.
Tensile or compression testing can evaluate the mechanical-property response to treatment.
Failure of combined treatments to produce statistically significant improvements over isolated-treatment controls would falsify the hypothesis.
